lead: Higher order linear ODEs look long, but they are built from two cheap pieces: a complementary function from the roots of a polynomial, and a particular integral from the shape of the right-hand side. This unit gives you both pieces — guessing rules, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters — plus the Wronskian test that says when solutions are genuinely independent. By the end you can solve constant-coefficient and Cauchy-Euler equations of any order, handle a second-order equation with variable coefficients, and read a pair of first-order equations as a phase portrait with stable and unstable critical points.
about: This unit is about linear ODEs of second and higher order — equations in which y and its derivatives appear only to the first power, with no products like yy′. Chapter 2.1 solves the constant-coefficient homogeneous case from the characteristic equation; 2.2 and 2.4 build a particular integral by guessing its shape and matching constants; 2.3 supplies the Wronskian test for independence. Chapter 2.5 replaces guessing by integration for any right-hand side, 2.6 handles the one variable-coefficient family that still solves exactly, and 2.8 the rest. Chapter 2.7 treats simultaneous equations, and 2.9 reads a pair of first-order equations as motion in the phase plane, with stability decided by eigenvalues.

chapters.idea: Put y = e^(mx) into the homogeneous equation, and the ODE collapses into a polynomial whose roots hand you the whole solution.
chapters.depth: Write the equation as aₙy⁽ⁿ⁾ + … + a₁y′ + a₀y = f(x), where each aᵢ is a constant, aₙ ≠ 0, and n is the order. For f = 0, substitute y = e^(mx) and cancel e^(mx); what is left is the characteristic equation (also called the auxiliary equation) aₙmⁿ + … + a₁m + a₀ = 0, a polynomial of degree n with n roots. Distinct real roots m₁, …, mₙ give C₁e^(m₁x) + … + Cₙe^(mₙx). A root m repeated r times gives e^(mx)(C₁ + C₂x + … + Cᵣx^(r−1)). A complex pair α ± iβ gives e^(αx)(C₁cos βx + C₂sin βx). The result is the complementary function (C.F.); it carries n arbitrary constants. Stay with the homogeneous case here.

figure.title: From ODE to complementary function
figure.aria: A downward flow from the homogeneous constant-coefficient ODE to its characteristic equation, then to the roots, which split into three branches: distinct real roots, a repeated root and a complex pair.
figure.caption: One polynomial of degree n, three kinds of root, three shapes of complementary function.

chapters.example: Solve y‴ − 6y″ + 11y′ − 6y = 0. The characteristic equation is m³ − 6m² + 11m − 6 = 0. m = 1 works (1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0), so divide by (m − 1): m² − 5m + 6 = (m − 2)(m − 3). The roots are 1, 2, 3, all real and distinct, so y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ + C₃e³ˣ.
chapters.trap: Writing two separate exponential terms for a repeated root instead of the x-multiplied form, and dropping the e^(αx) factor when the roots come as a complex pair.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for first-order linear equations; school-level complex numbers and quadratic roots.
chapters.leave: Non-homogeneous particular integrals to 2.2 and 2.4; variable coefficients to 2.6 and 2.8; power series solutions to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: For a right-hand side made of an exponential, a sine, a cosine or a polynomial, the particular integral has the same shape — just read the constants off.
chapters.depth: Write D for d/dx, so the equation is f(D)y = R(x). For R = e^(ax), the particular integral is e^(ax)/f(a) provided f(a) ≠ 0. If f(a) = 0, multiply by x: use x·e^(ax)/f′(a), and repeat if a is a double root. For R = sin(ax + b) or cos(ax + b), replace every D² by −a² and simplify; if the denominator becomes zero, multiply the trial by x. For a polynomial, either expand 1/f(D) as a series in D up to the degree of the polynomial, or fall back on the trial method of 2.4. For a sum of such terms, add the separate answers. Some syllabi call these the inverse-operator rules and the zero-denominator case the failure case.

figure.aria: A flow that inspects the right-hand side, sorts it into exponential, trigonometric or polynomial, then checks whether the trial already solves the homogeneous equation before substituting.
figure.caption: The shape of the right-hand side fixes the trial; a clash with the complementary function adds a factor x.

chapters.example: Solve y″ − 3y′ + 2y = e^(3x) + x. Roots of m² − 3m + 2 = 0 are 1 and 2, so the C.F. is C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ. Neither 3 nor 0 is a root, so no clash. For e^(3x) try A e^(3x): 9A − 9A + 2A = 1 gives A = 1/2. For x try Bx + C: 0 − 3B + 2(Bx + C) = x gives 2B = 1, so B = 1/2, and −3B + 2C = 0, so C = 3/4. Hence y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ + (1/2)e^(3x) + x/2 + 3/4.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the ×x when the exponent or frequency already appears in the C.F. — e^(2x) against roots 1 and 2 needs Axe^(2x), not Ae^(2x) — and using a lone cos or a lone sin instead of the pair.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1, especially the roots of the characteristic equation.
chapters.leave: Products of terms and repeated clashes to 2.4; right-hand sides that are none of these four shapes to 2.5.

chapters.idea: The Wronskian is a single determinant that answers yes or no to the question: are these solutions really independent?
chapters.depth: Solutions y₁, …, yₙ on an interval I are linearly dependent if constants cᵢ, not all zero, make c₁y₁ + … + cₙyₙ = 0 on the whole interval; otherwise they are independent. The Wronskian puts the functions in the first row and each successive derivative in the next row, and takes the determinant; for two functions W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂. A nonzero W at even one point of I proves independence. For solutions of a linear ODE, Abel's formula gives W = W₀ exp(−∫P dx), so W is either zero everywhere on I or nowhere — one value settles the whole interval. n independent solutions form a fundamental set, and every solution is a linear combination of them. n initial conditions at one point fix the n constants uniquely.

figure.title: Wronskian of two solutions
figure.aria: A two-row table holding the two solutions in the first row and their derivatives in the second, whose determinant is the Wronskian.
figure.caption: The determinant of this little table is W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂; one nonzero value anywhere proves independence.

chapters.example: Take y₁ = eˣ and y₂ = e²ˣ. Then W = eˣ(2e²ˣ) − eˣ(e²ˣ) = e³ˣ, which is never zero, so the pair is independent. Take y₁ = x and y₂ = 3x. Then W = x(3) − (1)(3x) = 0 everywhere, so the pair is dependent.
chapters.trap: Reading W = 0 at a single point as dependence. For solutions of a linear ODE the Wronskian is zero everywhere or nowhere, so one nonzero value is enough — but that shortcut fails for arbitrary functions.
chapters.leave: Orthogonality and Sturm-Liouville theory to Unit 3; the reduction-of-order formula to 2.8.

chapters.idea: Write a trial solution with unknown constants whose shape matches the right-hand side, then substitute and compare coefficients term by term.
chapters.depth: The method of undetermined coefficients is the bookkeeping version of 2.2, and it covers products and sums. Rules: a polynomial of degree n needs a full polynomial with n+1 constants, lower-degree terms included. e^(ax) times a polynomial needs e^(ax) times the full polynomial. A lone sin ax or cos ax needs A cos ax + B sin ax, always both. A product of two shapes needs the product of the two trials. A sum of terms needs the sum of the trials. If a piece of the trial already solves the homogeneous equation, multiply the whole trial by x, as many times as that root repeats in the characteristic equation. The method works only for constant-coefficient equations whose right-hand side is built from polynomials, exponentials, sines, cosines and their products.

figure.aria: A decision tree that starts from the right-hand side and branches into polynomial, exponential-times-polynomial and trigonometric trials, with a repair branch that multiplies the trial by a power of x.
figure.caption: Each branch of the tree gives the trial; the two repair boxes multiply it by x when the trial already solves the homogeneous equation.

chapters.example: Solve y″ − y = x². The characteristic equation m² − 1 = 0 gives roots ±1, so the C.F. is C₁eˣ + C₂e⁻ˣ. Since 0 is not a root, try y_p = Ax² + Bx + C, so y_p″ = 2A. Substituting: 2A − Ax² − Bx − C = x². Comparing: −A = 1, so A = −1; −B = 0, so B = 0; 2A − C = 0, so C = −2. Hence y = C₁eˣ + C₂e⁻ˣ − x² − 2.
chapters.trap: Trying only the top term (Ax² for a right-hand side of x²) and leaving out the lower-degree constants; and not multiplying by x when the trial is already part of the C.F.
chapters.leave: General right-hand sides and variable coefficients to 2.5; forced oscillations and resonance in vibrating systems to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Let the two constants in the complementary function become functions of x, impose two conditions, and integrate to get the particular integral — no guessing needed.
chapters.depth: Start with y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = R(x) and its C.F. y_c = C₁y₁ + C₂y₂. Replace the constants by functions and write y_p = u₁(x)y₁ + u₂(x)y₂. Impose two conditions. The first, u₁′y₁ + u₂′y₂ = 0, keeps y_p″ free of u₁″ and u₂″. The second, u₁′y₁′ + u₂′y₂′ = R, comes from making y_p satisfy the ODE. Solving the pair gives u₁′ = −y₂R/W and u₂′ = y₁R/W, where W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂. Integrate both and drop the constants of integration, since the C.F. already carries them. If the equation arrives as a₀(x)y″ + a₁(x)y′ + a₂(x)y = f(x), divide by a₀ first: the numerators then carry f/a₀ instead of R. Works for any continuous right-hand side and for variable coefficients; the price is two integrals.

figure.title: Variation of parameters, step by step
figure.aria: A flow from the complementary function and its Wronskian into the two derivative formulas for u₁ and u₂, then into the two integrals and finally into the particular integral.
figure.caption: The Wronskian sits in the denominator of both formulas; the two integrals give the particular integral directly.

chapters.example: Solve y″ + y = sec x for 0 < x < π/2. Here y₁ = cos x, y₂ = sin x and W = cos²x + sin²x = 1, with R = sec x and a₀ = 1. Then u₁′ = −sin x·sec x = −tan x, so u₁ = ln|cos x|; and u₂′ = cos x·sec x = 1, so u₂ = x. Therefore y = C₁cos x + C₂sin x + cos x·ln|cos x| + x sin x.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to divide by the leading coefficient a₀(x) before naming the right-hand side, and losing the minus sign in u₁′ = −y₂R/W.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.3; standard integrals and integration by parts.
chapters.leave: Numerical evaluation of the integrals, and Runge-Kutta or finite-difference solutions, to a numerical methods course.

chapters.idea: When the coefficients are powers of x that match the derivative order, the substitution x = e^t turns the equation into one with constant coefficients.
chapters.depth: A Cauchy-Euler equation (also called Euler-Cauchy or equidimensional) has the form aₙxⁿy⁽ⁿ⁾ + … + a₁xy′ + a₀y = f(x). For x > 0 put x = e^t, so t = ln x, and write θ = d/dt. Then xy′ = θy, x²y″ = θ(θ − 1)y, and x³y‴ = θ(θ − 1)(θ − 2)y. The equation becomes constant-coefficient in t, solved by 2.1 and 2.2, and every e^(kt) is then written back as x^k. For x < 0 work with |x|. The Legendre linear form has powers of (a + bx): put a + bx = e^t, and then (a + bx)y′ = bθy. A shortcut for the homogeneous part is to try y = x^m, which gives the same indicial equation.

figure.title: Turning a Cauchy-Euler equation into a constant-coefficient one
figure.aria: A straight flow that takes a Cauchy-Euler equation, applies the substitution x equals e to the t, solves the resulting constant-coefficient equation, and returns to x.
figure.caption: The substitution does all the work: powers of x become constants, and e to the kt becomes x to the k.

chapters.example: Solve x²y″ − 2xy′ + 2y = x³ for x > 0. With x = e^t, the left side becomes θ(θ − 1)y − 2θy + 2y = (θ² − 3θ + 2)y, and the right side becomes e^(3t). The roots of m² − 3m + 2 are 1 and 2, so the C.F. is C₁e^t + C₂e^(2t) = C₁x + C₂x². For e^(3t) try Ae^(3t): (9 − 9 + 2)A = 1, so A = 1/2. Hence y = C₁x + C₂x² + x³/2.
chapters.trap: Writing x²y″ = θ²y instead of θ(θ − 1)y; and using ln x without noting that the substitution needs x > 0.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2; laws of indices and logarithms.
chapters.leave: Legendre polynomials and Legendre's equation to Unit 3 — a different topic with a similar name; general series solutions also to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Two or more coupled linear equations in the same variable can be combined into one higher-order equation by elimination.
chapters.depth: The system has two or more unknown functions of one variable t, constant coefficients, and D = d/dt, for example Dx + 2y = 3t and 3x + Dy = 0. Elimination method: apply a suitable operator to one equation, substitute the other into it, and land on a single higher-order ODE in one unknown. Solve that, then back-substitute to get the second unknown. The number of arbitrary constants equals the total order of the system — two constants for two first-order equations. Keep to two equations and two unknowns. Only a few universities teach this topic.

figure.title: Elimination for a simultaneous pair
figure.aria: A flow that takes a coupled pair, eliminates one unknown to leave a single higher-order equation, solves it, and substitutes back for the other unknown.
figure.caption: Elimination trades two first-order equations for one second-order equation, then recovers the second unknown.

chapters.example: Solve dx/dt = y, dy/dt = x. Differentiate the first equation and substitute the second: d²x/dt² = dy/dt = x, so x″ − x = 0. The roots of m² − 1 are ±1, giving x = C₁e^t + C₂e⁻ᵗ. Then y = dx/dt = C₁e^t − C₂e⁻ᵗ.
chapters.trap: Reporting only one arbitrary constant instead of two, and stopping after finding x without substituting back for y.
chapters.leave: Matrix and Laplace-transform methods for systems to later courses; the phase-plane picture of the same system to 2.9.

chapters.idea: With variable coefficients, one known solution buys you the second by integration, and variation of parameters then supplies the particular integral.
chapters.depth: Put the equation in standard form y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = R(x) by dividing by the leading coefficient. If one nonzero solution y₁ is known, reduction of order gives y₂ = y₁∫ e^(−∫P dx)/y₁² dx, and y₁, y₂ are independent; the Wronskian is W = W₀e^(−∫P dx) by Abel's identity. The complementary function is C₁y₁ + C₂y₂, and the particular integral follows from 2.5 on the same standard form. Closed forms exist only for special families: Cauchy-Euler (2.6), or equations a substitution reduces to constant coefficients. Everything else needs a power series about an ordinary point (Unit 3) or a numerical method such as fourth-order Runge-Kutta or finite differences.

figure.title: One solution buys the second
figure.aria: A flow from one known solution through the reduction-of-order integral to the second solution, then into the Wronskian, then into variation of parameters for the particular integral.
figure.caption: One solution plus one integration gives the second; the rest is the chapter 2.5 machinery.

chapters.example: Given that y₁ = x solves x²y″ + xy′ − y = 0, find the second solution and then solve x²y″ + xy′ − y = x². Standard form: y″ + (1/x)y′ − (1/x²)y = 0, so P = 1/x and e^(−∫P dx) = 1/x. Then y₂ = x∫ (1/x)/x² dx = x∫x⁻³dx = −1/(2x), so take y₂ = 1/x. For the full equation, R = 1 and W = x(−1/x²) − (1)(1/x) = −2/x. Then u₁′ = −(1/x)(1)/(−2/x) = 1/2, so u₁ = x/2; and u₂′ = x(1)/(−2/x) = −x²/2, so u₂ = −x³/6. Hence y_p = x²/2 − x²/6 = x²/3 and y = C₁x + C₂/x + x²/3.
chapters.trap: Using the reduction-of-order formula on a₀y″ + a₁y′ + a₂y = f without dividing first — P must be a₁/a₀, not a₁.
chapters.leave: Power series and the Frobenius method to Unit 3; Runge-Kutta 4 and finite differences to a numerical methods course.

chapters.idea: Plot y against x instead of against t: the points where both derivatives vanish are critical points, and their eigenvalues decide whether nearby motion falls in, spirals around, or runs away.
chapters.depth: An autonomous system is x′ = F(x, y), y′ = G(x, y) with no t on the right. Time is hidden, so a solution is a curve in the xy-plane, the phase plane. A critical point (equilibrium point) solves F = G = 0. Linearise there: the Jacobian is J = [[F_x, F_y], [G_x, G_y]]. Its eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂ decide the picture through τ = λ₁ + λ₂ = trace J and Δ = λ₁λ₂ = det J. Δ < 0 gives a saddle, always unstable. Δ > 0 with τ² > 4Δ gives a node, stable if τ < 0. Δ > 0 with τ² < 4Δ gives a spiral, stable if τ < 0. τ = 0 with Δ > 0 gives a centre, with closed curves around it. Stable means nearby solutions stay near, and for a stable node or spiral approach the critical point as t → ∞.

figure.aria: A phase portrait with a critical point at the centre, arrows on the vertical axis pointing in towards it and arrows on the horizontal axis pointing away from it.
figure.caption: The critical point at the centre: motion along the vertical is pulled in, motion along the horizontal is pushed out — a saddle.

chapters.example: For the system x′ = x, y′ = −2y, the only critical point is (0, 0). The Jacobian is [[1, 0], [0, −2]], so λ₁ = 1, λ₂ = −2, giving τ = −1 and Δ = −2 < 0: a saddle, unstable. Solving directly gives x = C₁e^t and y = C₂e⁻²ᵗ, so yx² = constant — the trajectories are hyperbola-like curves running out along x and in along y.
chapters.trap: Trusting the linearised classification when Δ = 0 or an eigenvalue has zero real part, where higher-order terms decide; and calling a saddle stable because one eigenvalue is negative.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for characteristic roots and eigenvalues; Unit 1 for first-order equations.
chapters.leave: Limit cycles and nonlinear stability proofs to advanced courses; the elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic classification of PDEs to Unit 5, where the same words mean something different.
